# Human Framework at 08aab973: independent direction review

## Verdict and what I inspected

**Verdict: worth continued investment only as a small, auditable agent harness plus a disciplined research notebook. Not worth investment as a "reusable human framework," and not yet a game anyone would choose to play.** The engineering is unusually honest and the negative results are preserved, which is rare and valuable. But the executable model is a five-action utility scorer wrapped around one authored resource task. The project's own follow-up experiment shows the flagship "Full" policy is matched by a two-threshold rule. The social mechanism never fires under the shipped policy. The Islamic grounding is currently expressed almost entirely by absence. The right move is to shrink the claimed scope to what the code actually does well, extract that into a host-independent harness, and put the human-modeling ambition into narrow pre-registered discrimination tests with stopping rules.

**Evidence inspected.** README, the framework proposal, roadmap, model reference, MVP spec, coverage ledger, validation program, capacity fix, benchmark report and its 0.1 archive, recovery exploration, all research memos, all of `src/core`, `src/scenarios`, `src/experiments.js`, the frozen 0.1 kernel, `web/app.js`, `web/guidance.js`, `index.html`, all nine test files, the build and serve scripts, and the benchmark and recovery-probe artifacts by targeted search.

**Evidentiary limits.** I could not run code, so every numerical claim below is read from committed artifacts or derived by hand from the scoring formulas. I could not check any citation. Four documents referenced from the snapshot are absent: the post-MVP direction review, the MVP status record, the deployment workflow and the earlier review record. They are cited at README.md:11, README.md:102, roadmap.md:3, decision-status.md:28 and validation-program.md:3. I do not infer their contents.

## Findings

**1. Value proposition and audience.** The differentiators are not in the decision policy. The Full policy is a deterministic weighted sum with an ID tie-break at policy.js:9-46, which is ordinary utility AI. What is genuinely distinctive lives around it:

- The actor view excludes hidden hazard, seed and peer priorities, and a test proves changing hidden hazard alone cannot change the plan. See observation.js:7-21 and core.test.js:18-28.
- Request and execution are recorded separately, with the declared intention preserved when capacity substitutes recovery. See simulation.js:107-131 and capacity.test.js:11-31.
- Draws are keyed by seed, round, actor and purpose, so unrelated activity cannot consume simulation randomness. See random.js and core.test.js:70-76.
- Every score carries labeled contributions that the UI renders as bars. See policy.js:10-11 and app.js:297-300.

A game author gains an information-hygiene and audit contract, not behavior. The compelling use case is therefore a game where what a character believed versus what was true is the mechanic: a witness or testimony game, a small management game where the player must not be able to read NPC internals, or a teaching tool for model comparison. The framework should deliberately not be used for anything real-time with many agents, anything needing multi-step planning, anything needing negotiation or emotion, and, importantly, anything marketed as spiritual formation. None of those exist in code.

As three artifacts: the research notebook is strong. The developer library is nascent because the world lives inside the kernel. The game is four reskins of one aggregate-progress task, which README.md:32 admits.

**2. Alternative model structures.** The five "modules" at model.js:2 are boolean flags threaded through one monolithic resolver and one ranking function, not owners of state. The beliefs flag is checked in both simulation.js:75 and policy.js:32. The relationships flag appears at simulation.js:82, 92, 139 and policy.js:18, 37. Adding one action kind requires edits to the validator, resolver, policy and guidance. The world schema is fixed to progress, food and hazard at simulation.js:13. So the current decomposition wraps one production game rather than matching causal responsibilities. The proposal's own correction at framework-proposal.md:180 concedes the kernel still owns the world and all turns.

Two serious alternatives:

- **Much smaller: an agent harness.** Keep only view projection, a choice-provider interface, an attempt validator with the capacity query, the decision record, and keyed replay. Drop the world, the five flags and the Full policy. The host supplies actions with declared costs and effects. This is what survives if the universal ambition fails, and it is what the tests already protect best.
- **Same size, different owners.** A body process that is a pure function of elapsed minutes and effort. A generic evidence store rather than one hazard estimate. A commitment ledger with make, keep, break and release events owned between actors, replacing the single authored promise field per actor at model.js:75-79. A function-valued policy replacing the two-value enum at model.js:93.

I do not recommend a cognitive architecture. Soar or ACT-R would add nothing to a task with five actions, and the prior-art memo's advice to run policies behind one interface at prior-art-mvp.md:26 is unmet by the current code, where step calls rankActions directly at simulation.js:103.

**3. Incentives and experiments.** The benchmark cannot separate competence from realism, and mostly measures neither.

- The baseline is a never-plan controller. Its work score is at least output times 0.35, which exceeds its fixed rest and eat scores of 0.25 and 0.2 for every shipped work action. See policy.js:16. Any policy that ever rests beats it on forced recoveries by construction. The report concedes this at benchmark-report.md:34.
- The stronger comparator answers the question. At the 24-round Solo pressure profile, planned-simple and Full each win 75 of 100 evaluation seeds, and 81 versus 82 on seeds 1001 to 1100. See recovery-design-exploration.md:21-26 and the probe artifact at lines 3742 and 4813. Under an 18-round deadline greedy beats both. That is a defensible counterexample: Full rests on a quadratic fatigue term with no deadline awareness, so it under-pushes when a human would push.
- Full can look better for a reason unrelated to human modeling. Its forecast at policy.js:18 calls the same logistic that resolves outcomes at model.js:109-113, with only body perception coarsened and hazard estimated. The agent knows the world's equation.
- The environment inflates progress. All actors finish the round before termination, so overshoot favors larger contributions. See simulation.js:143 and benchmark-report.md:43. Completion sits at ceiling, so the primary metric has no discriminating power.
- The relationships module is inert. The full-minus-without-relationships comparison has a paired standard error of exactly zero in all four scenarios. See benchmark.json lines 21360-21400, 45545, 69730 and 93915. By my reading of policy.js:35-38, help can score at most roughly 0.77 for the highest authored care weight, while careful work typically exceeds 1.0 and rest dominates at high fatigue. Help is never selected, so trust updates at simulation.js:92 and 139 never influence anything. "No objective effect" at README.md:82 understates this: the ablation tests nothing.
- Water Commons does not exercise its advertised decision. Without-commitments is identical to Full in every metric there. See benchmark.json:69366-69406. That is only consistent with Meryem's authored help promise at scenarios/index.js:59 expiring in every seed. The README table at line 29 lists "prepare assistance and keep commitments" as decisions this preset exposes. Under the auto policy it exposes neither. I could not run the scenario to confirm.
- Metrics omit the social and epistemic outcomes. The summary at experiments.js:31-59 has no help count, no trust, no belief error. Realism is unmeasured, and cannot be measured against synthetic outputs anyway.

Separately scored: policy competence is parity with two thresholds. Realism is unmeasured and arguably worse under deadline. Authoring usefulness is unmeasured with a single author. Theological fidelity is a property of the documents, not the code. Enjoyable play is unmeasured. The 400 of 400 null pairs at benchmark.json:24371 verify pairing plumbing only, which the report says correctly.

**4. The human and religious premise.** Inspectable code facts first. No religious variable exists in `src`. Intention is a free string, capped at 1000 characters and never parsed. See simulation.js:21 and 106. A test proves two intentions yield identical worlds at adversarial.test.js:15-23. The UI offers five canned intentions at index.html:72. Duty is a scalar multiplier on a promise bonus at policy.js:41-42. A promise is fulfilled by one execution before its due round regardless of outcome, at simulation.js:91. Perception bias exists at observation.js:4 but no shipped actor sets it. There is no morally weighted action in the vocabulary and no prohibited-but-possible act.

Interpretive judgments. The restraint is real and, I think, correct: no piety meter, no soul units, no Arabic-named floats, exactly as decision-status.md:13 and the foundations memo argue. Representing less is more faithful for ruh, qadar and divine acceptance. But it is evasive for the two distinctions the project advertises as implemented. Intention "matters" only in the sense that it is stored. Nothing in play or in any character's record can depend on it, so it cannot be right, wrong, sincere or mixed. And duty is implemented as exactly the morality-as-reward the proposal warns against at framework-proposal.md:192: a promise competes with hunger squared in one utility sum. The test that a hungry actor can still keep a commitment passes because the bonus is large enough, not because obligation is represented differently from appetite.

The sharpest way to say it: if every noninstrumental reason vanished from play tomorrow, nothing would change, because none is implemented. The promise term is instrumental. The project's distinctive premise is not load-bearing.

Questions needing qualified scholarship, which I cannot adjudicate: whether a promise as a due-date bonus misrepresents ʿahd; whether "duty" as a personal preference weight misrepresents obligation; how the record for a prohibited-but-possible act should be labeled. The validation program already names these at validation-program.md:59-63.

**5. Product and integration reality.** The documented API cannot host a separate game today.

- One command per round, one player-controlled actor. See simulation.js:97-103 and mvp-spec.md:18. A host cannot drive two players, inject an external observation or deliver an outcome.
- No target field on commands. Help selects its recipient by perceived fatigue at simulation.js:79. Target-specific actions do not exist.
- Time is fixed per scenario and every step advances exactly one round. Host-owned time does not exist.
- The world is engine state. A separate game means editing the resolver.

Highest-risk mismatches between claims and code:

- "Reusable components" at README.md:3 with zero external reuse.
- "Model components 5 / 5" at index.html:43 when one never fires and body-off still enforces capacity.
- "Full is a replaceable reactive policy" at roadmap.md:50 when the policy option is a two-value enum.
- The README leads at line 80 with Full-versus-baseline progress that the project's own exploration shows is uninformative, while parity with planned-simple is buried at roadmap.md:59.
- The public build ships the frozen 0.1 kernel at build.js:20, dead weight for players.

Player feedback is thoughtful: perceived-body capacity warnings at guidance.js:26, request-versus-executed markup, contribution bars. But contributions are arbitrary utility units per model-reference.md:74, so a player sees legible arithmetic rather than legible reasons. Only a playtest can say whether that reads as explanation.

Evidence static inspection cannot supply: a second consumer in a separate repository with a measured zero-diff on core; think-aloud playtests on forced recovery; runtime at ten thousand events; a unit-invariance test that multiplies outputs by ten and shows whether choices change, which decision-status.md:28 says they do.

## Direction: retain, cut, replace, defer

| Decision | Item | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Retain | View projection, request/execution record, keyed RNG, replay, JSON validation, tests | The genuine contribution; well tested |
| Retain | Solo Repair, planned-simple comparator, research memos, decision register | Controls and honest records |
| Cut | Full versus greedy as headline evidence | Answered; greedy is a never-plan controller |
| Cut | Relationships module as shipped | Causally inert under the shipped policy |
| Cut | Two of the three two-person presets; 0.1 kernel from the public build | Reskins; maintenance cost without evidence value |
| Replace | Two-value policy enum | Function-valued choice provider |
| Replace | Single authored promise per actor | Commitment ledger with events, only when a host needs it |
| Replace | "Grounded in Islam" top line | "Designed under Islamic constraints" until positive representation exists |
| Defer | Active inference, cognitive architectures, emotion, memory, macro models, theology at runtime | Correctly shelved at roadmap.md:40-44 |

**Roadmap critique.** The four gates are sensible in spirit but gate 1 is open-ended research with no stopping rule, and its central question is already answered. Gate 2 is a rewrite presented as an extraction, because there is no event interface to extract. Gate 3's playtest is right. Gate 4 is right. The roadmap keeps Full as the default and keeps four presets as controls; three are reskins.

**Feasible sequence with stopping rules.**

1. **Harness extraction.** Freeze the kernel. Write the harness from the retained pieces with no world fields in its state. Stop rule: if it cannot be expressed in roughly two hundred lines without a world schema, the abstraction is not there and the project is a notebook.
2. **Authoring test.** Someone other than the maintainer builds the two-location workshop with inventory, travel and a deadline in a separate repository, using the harness and a plain host-native controller for NPCs. Pass: zero core edits, targeted actions and variable durations expressed as host events, save-and-resume identical. Fail: any new kind added to the enum at model.js:61 or any world field added to engine state. A fail ends the library line and keeps only the notebook.
3. **Gameplay test.** Five-person playtest of that host game with policy hints hidden. Pass: four explain the objective, one tradeoff and the cause of one forced recovery, and at least three choose a second run unprompted. Fail: stop game investment; the harness is a research instrument.
4. **Model-discrimination test.** On the 24-round Solo profile, pre-register three controllers: two thresholds, two thresholds plus deadline awareness, and Full. Evaluate on seeds 1001 to 1100 without retuning. I predict the deadline-aware threshold rule matches or beats Full. If so, retire Full as default and keep it as an example policy. A realism test is a separate track and the current body model cannot support the one affordable candidate, the sleepiness-versus-performance dissociation cited at roadmap.md:21, because perception is exact rounding. Add a fatigue-dependent perception gap; if it changes no decision, remove it.
5. **Theological increment.** One reviewed scenario with a prohibited-but-possible act and one noninstrumental reason whose only effect is on the character's own record. Pass gate: a qualified Hanafi-Maturidi reviewer accepts the record labels, not the outcomes. Stop rule: if no reviewer is obtainable within the increment, theology stays a constraints document.

Success in the authoring test does not prove the gameplay test, and neither says anything about realism. The increments are ordered so each can end a line of work cheaply.

**Competing direction.** Build one small single-player testimony game. The player is one of several agents with private observations and must decide what to inspect, what to report and whom to trust. NPCs use the planned-simple policy. The harness's projection and intention record become the game's mechanic rather than its plumbing. This is the strongest honest version of the project because it makes the actual differentiator visible to a player. The strongest external rival is Ensemble plus utility AI inside an existing engine, which gives an author social rules and legible behavior today with no research program attached.

**Strongest objection to my recommendation.** Cutting Full and the relationships module removes the only parts that make this more than a harness, and a harness is a commodity. The ambition is the reason the work exists. My answer is that the ambition is not cut but relocated into pre-registered discrimination tests, which need a good harness and a strong comparator more than they need a bigger Full. And "commodity" is itself testable: the authoring test will show whether a host author finds the harness worth importing.

**Unresolved questions.** Whether the omitted direction review contradicts this reading. Whether the author wants a game, a library or a research program, since the documents claim all three. Whether qualified theological review is actually obtainable. Whether any audience exists for a build-free JavaScript agent library. And the one thing I most wanted to run: whether help is ever chosen by the Full policy anywhere in the shipped presets.
